entries.title: Middle East updates: Kushner meets Netanyahu in Jerusalem
entries.summary: The meeting comes amid a stalled post-war Gaza plan and after an Israeli minister called for more Palestinians to be killed in the enclave. Meanwhile, Iran says it is finalizing a deal with Oman on the Strait of Hormuz.
entries.content:
Middle East

Middle East updates: Kushner meets Netanyahu in Jerusalem

August 17, 2026

The meeting comes amid a stalled post-war Gaza plan and after an Israeli minister called for more Palestinians to be killed in the enclave. Meanwhile, Iran says it is finalizing a deal with Oman on the Strait of Hormuz.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Israeli PM Netanyahu and US envoy Kushner meet in Jerusalem
  • Israeli minister calls for more "targeted killings" of Palestinians in the Gaza Strip
  • Iran says it "finalizing" a deal with Oman regarding the Strait of Hormuz

Welcome to DW's coverage of developments in the Middle East on Monday, 17 August, 2026.

Skip next section Iran working to finalize Hormuz agreement with Oman

Iran working to finalize Hormuz agreement with Oman

Iran's Foreign Ministry said Monday that it was working to finalize a joint statement with Oman on a plan to manage the passage of ships through the Strait of Hormuz.

"An understanding has been reached regarding the map of the transit route," said foreign affairs spokesman Esmail Baghaei, conceding that talks with Oman had progressed slowly.

"We had planned, and still plan, to finalize the understanding in the form of a package: the map plus a joint statement," he told reporters in Tehran.

Although Baghaei did not elaborate on the plan, previous details have suggested that ships could be expected to enter the key waterway through a route closer to Iran before exiting on a route closer to Oman. It is not expected that ships would have to pay fees or tolls.

The announcement came as a 60-day negotiating period to agree a permanent peace deal between the United States and Iran expired, with no word of an extension and both sides seemingly as far apart as they were two months ago.

The US has sought an acceptable deal on reopening the strait before ending its blockade of Iranian ports and it was not immediately clear whether the new Iran-Oman deal would meet Washington's expectations.

Skip next section Israeli minister calls for more 'targeted killings' in Gaza

Israeli minister calls for more 'targeted killings' in Gaza

Monday's meeting between Benjamin Netanyahu and US envoy Jared Kushner comes after Israel's national security minister called for dozens more Palestinians to be killed "every night" in "targeted killings" in the Gaza Strip.

Far-right hardliner Itamar Ben-Gvir made the remarks in a podcast with a former Gaza hostage which went live on Saturday evening.

"I think that targeted killings should be carried out in Gaza, removing 30, 40 people every night," he said, specifying that he was not only referring to members of militant groups.

"Not just those who pose an immediate threat; there are people there who are not worthy of life. They shouldn't live. They're not even people."

Ben-Gvir is the chairman of the "Otzma Yehudit" ("Jewish Power") party and a member of Netanyahu's government, but he said he disagrees with the prime minister's plans for post-war Gaza.

Meanwhile, Iran's deputy foreign minister condemned the comments in a post on social media on Monday morning.

"This Zionist criminal speaks at the same time of expelling Palestinians and of settlement construction across the entire Gaza Strip," wrote Kazem Gharibabadi. "These confessions must be recorded and preserved for the day of reckoning and for the trial of these criminals."

In the past, similar statements by Ben-Gvir and other Israeli officials have been presented to the UN's world court as evidence of genocidal intent. Israel denies that its actions in Gaza constitute genocide.

Skip next section Kushner meets Netanyahu in Jerusalem

Kushner meets Netanyahu in Jerusalem

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu hosted US President Donald Trump's envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner in Jerusalem on Monday as a US-backed plan for the governance of the Gaza Strip remained stalled.

The meeting, which comes a day after Kushner met with Hamas leader Khalil ‌Al-Hayya in Cairo, Egypt, was also attended by Trump's Board ‌of ​Peace envoy for Gaza, Nickolay Mladenov, and former British Prime Minister Tony Blair, according to media reports.

Earlier this month, Netanyahu publicly rejected a Trump proposal which would have seen the militant group Hamas disarm and Israeli troops withdraw from the Gaza Strip.

Trump had said the agreement would be carried out in phases, with Israeli forces gradually replaced in the devastated Palestinian territory by an "International ​Stabilization Force" which would work alongside a new Palestinian police force.

Hamas has said it agreed to the plan but the deal has stalled, with Netanyahu insisting that Israel's military will only withdraw once Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza have been completely disarmed.

Israeli troops continue to occupy about 60% of the enclave and Netanyahu has previously threatened to advance further.

Netanyahu is struggling in the polls ahead of an October 27 general election, with some surveys putting him behind centrist challenger Gadi Eisenkot.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello and welcome to DW's coverage of developments in the Middle East on Monday, 17 August, 2026.

US President Donald Trump's son-in-law and envoy Jared Kushner met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Monday as plans for post-war Gaza remain stalled.

The meeting came after Israel's national security minister called on more "targeted killings" of Palestinians in a podcast interview.

Meanwhile, Iran says it is working to finalize an agreement with Oman over the management of the Strait of Hormuz.

entries.title: Putin visited Kuril to 'punish' Japan over Ukraine stance
entries.summary: Analysts have said a visit by Russia's leader to a disputed island chain sent a "message" to Japan, which for decades has sought to reclaim control of the territory.
entries.content:
Japan

Putin visited Kuril to 'punish' Japan over Ukraine stance

August 17, 2026

Analysts have said a visit by Russia's leader to a disputed island chain sent a "message" to Japan, which for decades has sought to reclaim control of the territory.

The first-ever visit by Russian President Vladimir Putin to one of the disputed Kuril islands off the far northern tip of Japan last week triggered a swift and angry response from Tokyo.

Japan Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said in a social media post that Putin's visit was "absolutely unacceptable" while referring to the islands, which it calls the "Northern Territories" as "inherently Japanese territory."

Russia's Foreign Ministry said in response that the islands are an "integral part" of Russia.

The Kuril islands were seized by Soviet troops two weeks after Japan's official surrender ending World War II on August 15, 1945, with the 17,300 Japanese residents forced to leave over the following year.

Putin toured, a school, a hospital and industrial facilities on the island of Iturup, which Japan refers to as Etorofu. It also came just two days before the 81st anniversary of Japan's surrender at the end of World War II.

"This was clearly a message to Japan," said James Brown, a professor of international relations specializing in Russian affairs at the Tokyo campus of Temple University.

"Russia has been angered by Japan's support for Ukraine and for the closer ties that Tokyo has been building with European members of NATO," he told DW.

"So there is a clear desire to punish Japan," he said. "But there is also a domestic element to this … as a visit like this can generate patriotic support among Russians of all political stripes."

Russia and Japan's longstanding territorial row

Successive Japanese governments have consistently taken the position that the islands were illegally annexed, with the dispute so impacting bilateral ties that the two nations have yet to sign a formal peace treaty.

The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 and the subsequent economic hardships gave Japan renewed hope that Moscow could be convinced to return the islands in return for economic assistance or even joint development of the region.

Former Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe was arguably the most proactive Japanese leader on the issue, meeting with Putin on a number of occasions in an effort to convince the Russian leader to come around to Japan's way of thinking.

However, all of these diplomatic efforts came to naught, with Russia amending its constitution in 2020 to ban the ceding of any part of Russian territory to a foreign power. Moscow's relations with Japan, further deteriorated after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Toshimitsu Shigemura, a professor of politics at Tokyo's Waseda University, told DW that these latest developments are just another nail in the coffin for Japan's ambition concerning the islands.

"Tokyo has already summoned the Russian ambassador and made a formal diplomatic protest, but sanctions are already in place over the Ukraine war and I think it will be difficult for Japan to add more," Shigemura said.

"Japan is importing Russian energy and, because of the situation with Iran, that has become even more important, which leaves Tokyo in a relatively weak position," he added.

Putin tests Japan

Shigemura believes that Putin – potentially in consort with China and North Korea – is attempting to weaken Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi because of the firm line she has taken on security issues in the region. He added that Putin is aware that Takaichi's domestic poll numbers are softening likely assesses the Japanese leader will not respond more forcefully than a protest.

Shigemura added that Russia's revised constitution and deepening nationalist sentiment encouraged by state propaganda effectively makes it "impossible" for the islands to be returned to Japanese control.

"Putin may be weak now, but he is cooperating with China and North Korea to challenge Takaichi, who has few options," he said. "And even after Putin has gone, there will be no interest in a new Russian government to return the islands."

Brown agrees, saying that while a few "excitable commentators" in Japan will see Putin's eventual departure from the Kremlin as an opportunity, whomever ends up controlling Russia will be unlikely to align with Japan's territorial interests.

"It did not happen with the collapse of the Soviet Union and all through Russia's subsequent economic difficulties so I don't see any new Russian leader who comes in as countenancing returning the islands," he said.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Cooler destinations are drawing tourists — can nature cope?
entries.summary: With heat records continually being broken and southern summers getting hotter, travelers are heading north. Fragile ecosystems are paying the price.
entries.content:
August 17, 2026

With heat records continually being broken and southern summers getting hotter, travelers are heading north. Fragile ecosystems are paying the price.

A ridge with sweeping views across Jotunheimen, a mountain region in southern Norway, seemed like the perfect hiking route for tour operator Georg Sichelschmidt to bring visitors. Then locals informed him it was home to nesting eagles.

The trail remained open. But Sichelschmidt didn't want to disturb the apex predators at home in the massive peaks, dotted with turquoise lakes and glaciers.

"We decided not to use this trail anymore. We had to find another solution," said Sichelschmidt, who runs nature-based tourism company JVB travel.

Norway's right-to-roam rules, known as allemannsretten, give people broad access to nature regardless of land ownership but also require them to respect it. For Sichelschmidt, who moved from Germany to Norway 16 years ago for its nature, the decision was an easy choice.

But with climate change reshaping summer travel, protecting nature will require far more than individual decisions. According to a 2026 OECD tourism trends report, longer and more intense heat waves across southern Europe are helping drive interest in cooler destinations. That shift is raising concerns about whether nature in countries like Norway can withstand growing visitor numbers. 

Is the heat changing the way we travel?

The travel industry has coined the term "coolcation" to promote the shift in summer travel habits. It's too early to know how widespread the trend is, said Daniel Scott, a professor specializing in climate and tourism at Canada's University of Waterloo.

Booking companies, hotels, and airlines don't publish data showing how many travelers switch destinations because of heat alone, he said. Still, he added, "we know that people are thinking about it. Some say they are acting on it."

Sichelschmidt said he's seeing the trend firsthand. Partner tour operators offering trips to Mediterranean and the Nordic regions report growing interest in "active" northern vacations, such as hiking and biking, during summer.

"It is difficult to go hiking in France, Spain or Italy in July and August when it is 40 degrees [Celsius, 104 Fahrenheit] plus. The Nordics are a good option to escape from that," he said, adding that Mediterranean travel is shifting to spring and autumn. 

More visitors, more pressure on nature

Northern Norway already offers a glimpse of what rising visitor numbers can mean for fragile environments.

Lofoten, with its dramatic cliffs, deep fjords and wild beaches, is home to around 25,000 people. In 2025, it recorded more than 807,000 commercial guest nights, according to Statistics Norway. Increased interest in cooler vacations could add to existing pressure on nature there.

The archipelago is home to hundreds of bird species, including a colony of puffins that could be disturbed by growing visitor numbers. Nesting birds are vulnerable in late summer. But other wildlife can be impacted too, including reindeer during calving season in May and early June, said Elina Hutton, a tourism researcher at UiT The Arctic University of Norway. 

Lofoten's coastal heathland, bogs, and alpine vegetation are also highly vulnerable to foot traffic. When hikers walk on wet ground, they can damage roots and strip away the thin soil covering mountain bedrock. 

Using satellite data, Hutton tracks how growing visitor numbers are impacting trails on Lofoten. Along the route to Kvalvika Beach, an isolated bay only reachable by foot, the worst trails have widened to about 20 meters (65 feet), destroying surrounding vegetation. Northern ecosystems recover slowly from damage.

"That kind of damage is pretty much permanent here," said Hutton, who urged visitors to stick to established trails rather than seeking out "hidden gems" to post on social media.

Managing tourism, not just promoting it

Sichelschmidt believes tour operators can help reduce environmental harm by steering visitors onto well-managed trails, while avoiding the most sensitive areas.

"When we're talking about a large number of people, we need to direct them to where they can go so that the trails can be maintained without destroying nature," he added.

But decisions like Sichelschmidt's to avoid the eagle's nest cannot be left entirely to tour operators. Destinations will have to decide where visitors should go, which areas need greater protection, and how much pressure nature can sustain.

Norway is already experimenting with ways to manage tourism. Under a new law, communities facing particularly high tourism pressure will be allowed to charge a 3% accommodation tax starting in 2027. Hutton said the tax would not reduce visitor numbers but could help in other ways.

"At least it gives us a bit more tools, a bit more money to build better trails, to build better toilets and have better infrastructure to receive this number of tourists," she said.

Some countries are offering ecotourism initiatives that involve visitors in nature conservation work. In the Faroe Islands, for example, the "Closed for Maintenance" initiative invites volunteers to repair trails and maintain natural areas before they reopen to visitors

Still, destinations, municipalities and tourism businesses need to consider how many visitors they can accommodate and spread tourism evenly throughout the year, Hutton told DW. "It's not good for anybody if we just get more tourists," she said. 

Even 'cool' destinations are warming

But as humans continue to burn the fossil fuels heating the planet, the search for reliably cool destinations is becoming harder. Daniel Scott shared preliminary findings from an unpublished study with DW examining how heat risk is changing across Euromonitor's top 100 global city destinations. 

The research suggests tourists will increasingly be exposed to higher temperatures and more frequent heat-related risks. 

According to the analysis, only nine cities, including Dublin, Auckland and San Francisco, averaged fewer than 10 days per year with temperatures of 32C or higher between 2015 and 2025.

By the 2050s, that number is projected to fall by more than half, highlighting how even traditionally cooler destinations are expected to become significantly warmer.

Hutton finds it concerning to see destinations welcome tourism business opportunities created by Europe's extreme heat. "The same climate change impacts us too in one way or another, and no destination is going to be a winner when the situation evolves like this."

As more vacationers seek cooler weather, Sichelschmidt has decided not to use the term "coolcation" in his company's marketing.

"We don't want to use this situation for promotion," he said. "It's a real situation, but it's sad that we have to talk about it — or that we realize that we are destroying our planet and things change so fast."



Edited by: Jennifer Collins

entries.title: Germany's AfD is labeled far-right, populist or extremist
entries.summary: Right-wing, far-right, fascist: Many terms are being thrown around in the debate about the AfD. What do they mean, and how appropriate are they when discussing the AfD? DW has this glossary.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany's AfD is labeled far-right, populist or extremist

August 17, 2026

Right-wing, far-right, fascist: Many terms are being thrown around in the debate about the AfD. What do they mean, and how appropriate are they when discussing the AfD? DW has this glossary.

  • Far-right extremist

The Alternative for Germany (AfD) is often classified as a "far-right extremist party." However, the term has no clear-cut definition. In the broadest sense, it means that a party stands far to the right of the political center. Far-right parties are often associated with strong nationalism, racism, an authoritarian view of the state and a rejection of a liberal, pluralistic society.

Political scientist Armin Pfahl-Traughber of Germany's Federal University of Applied Administrative Sciences does not think that a far-right party is necessarily anti-democratic.

Speaking to DW, he explained why he considers the term "far-right extremist" more appropriate when discussing the AfD: "When it comes to the rejection of the fundamental values of a modern democracy — such as democracy, the separation of powers, human rights and pluralism — coupled with an overemphasis on ethnic identity, I use the label 'far-right extremist.'"

In his view, the AfD has undergone a transformation since its founding in 2013: "What began as a right-wing democratic party with a right-wing extremist minority has, over the years, developed into a right-wing extremist party with a right-wing democratic minority."

  • Right-wing populist

The word "populism" is derived from the Latin populus, which means "the people." Aside from that the term has no clear definition. It is frequently used to describe politicians or political parties who seek to curry favor with the masses.

According to Pfahl-Traughber, right-wing populism has several defining characteristics: It views the people as a single entity (and thus rejects pluralism), and it posits an opposition between "them" and "us," which usually means "the people" versus "the elites."

Furthermore, right-wing populists often seek to align themselves directly with the "common people" and claim to know what the people are thinking and demanding. The term is also frequently used to describe the AfD because its political style embodies these defining characteristics.

  • Right-wing conservative

The term "right-wing conservative" is usually applied to politicians or parties that emphasize the importance of conservative values such as homeland and the traditional family, as well as nationalism, a strong state and "law and order." Unlike right-wing extremists, they do not necessarily view the people as a racial or ethnic unity. They generally accept the fundamental principles of democracy and the existing constitutional order.

However, there have also been historical instances of anti-democratic movements emerging from right-wing conservatism: for example, the supporters of the Conservative Revolution in Germany, whose leading figures included Oswald Spengler, Ernst Jünger and Carl Schmitt. They rejected parliamentarism, modernity and social diversity, and called for a state ruled by an authoritarian leader. To this day, there are great admirers of these ideologues within the AfD and its circles. Björn Höcke, one of the most influential AfD politicians, for example, repeatedly refers to such thinkers in his book, "Nie zweimal in denselben Fluss" (Never in the same river twice).

  • völkisch

"Völkisch" is an adjectival form of the German noun, das Volk, or the people. However, since the late 19th century, das Volk has been used to refer to an ethnically pure community and has been strongly antisemitic from the outset. The völkisch movement was a precursor to the murderous National Socialism under Adolf Hitler. His party, the NSDAP, named its official party newspaper the "Völkischer Beobachter" (The Völkisch Observer).

Today, politicians and experts accuse the AfD of holding völkisch views because its officials repeatedly distinguish between Germans with and without a history of migration.

Armin Pfahl-Traughber believes that today it is a "vaguely defined concept that is used excessively."

  • fascist

The word describes an extreme political posture that invokes a nationalist, anti-democratic worldview. The term is derived from the Italian word fascio, or "bundle." Originally, it was the self-designation of the movement surrounding the Italian dictator Benito Mussolini in the early 20th century. Key characteristics of fascism under Mussolini included ultranationalism, the endorsement of the principle of a leader, the rejection of democracy and the glorification of violence and war. German National Socialism under Adolf Hitler drew on the Italian fascist movement and was later classified by historians as an extreme form of fascism.

The applicability of the term to far-right extremist movements today is a matter of debate among scholars.

"In most cases, the groups in question cannot be equated with Hitler or Mussolini's movements," argues Pfahl-Traughber.

In Germany, it is legal to refer to AfD politician Björn Höcke as a "fascist" because a court ruled that this would constitute a value judgment that rests on "verifiable facts."

  • 'suspected case of right-wing extremism'

This label is used by Germany's domestic intelligence agency, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution, and the AfD has been classified in Germany as a suspected case of right-wing extremism.

Pfahl-Traughber explains this classification to DW: "This means that there are actual grounds for suspecting an intention to undermine the free democratic basic order and that these grounds require further investigation."

For a party to be classified as a suspected case, it is not sufficient for it to merely hold anti-constitutional views.

The decisive factor is whether a party is planning to take actions that go against the fundamental values of society. According to findings by the Office for the Protection of the Constitution, the AfD's efforts to assign a legally inferior status to Germans with a migration background constitute such actions because it violates the German constitution. This ruling was upheld in 2024 by the Higher Administrative Court of Münster.

  • 'confirmed right-wing extremist'

According to political scientist Pfahl-Traughber, this classification by the Office for the Protection of the Constitution is "the result of an assessment concluding that the political actor is indeed considered extremist."

In Germany, the classification has consequences, meaning "a party may henceforth be monitored using intelligence agency methods." This means it may be monitored via telephone or observed by informants.

Furthermore, members of a party classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" may be denied employment as teachers, police officers or soldiers because their loyalty to the constitution cannot be guaranteed. The Office for the Protection of the Constitution's classification of the AfD as "confirmed right-wing extremist" is currently being reviewed by the Cologne Administrative Court.

This text was translated from German.

entries.title: DRC Ebola outbreak becomes deadliest in country's history
entries.summary: An Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has now killed 2,325 people, according to government figures. The UN says one person in the country is dying every 30 minutes of the disease.
entries.content:
Democratic Republic of Congo

DRC Ebola outbreak becomes deadliest in country's history

August 17, 2026

An Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has now killed 2,325 people, according to government figures. The UN says one person in the country is dying every 30 minutes of the disease.

An Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has now killed 2,325 people, surpassing a previous record toll of 2,299 from an outbreak in 2018-2020, government figures showed on Monday.

The deaths were from 4,945 confirmed cases of the disease, which is transmitted via infected bodily fluids and can cause fever, vomiting, diarrhea and, in severe cases, internal and external bleeding.

 The United Nations says the outbreak "is the fastest growing on record" and is killing a victim every half an hour in the DRC.

The outbreak is now second in lethality only to one in West Africa in 2014-2016.

At that time, 28,616 cases and 11,310 deaths were recorded across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra ​Leone, according ‌to the World Health Organization.

How has the Ebola outbreak spread in DRC?

The current outbreak, DRC's 17th, ‌is caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola.

There are no approved vaccines or treatments for the disease.

The outbreak, which was declared on May 15, began — probably several weeks earlier — in northeastern Ituri province and has now spread to five more provinces.

High rate of fatalities

The case fatality ratio — the proportion of deaths following a confirmed infection — has risen from some 20% in early June to 46% now, government data has shown.

That means that nearly one in two confirmed cases ends in death.

Experts say this rise does not suggest that the virus has become more lethal but instead reflects deficiencies in surveillance, detection and access to care.

The disease has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past 50 years.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Indonesia: Thousands await aid as quake death toll rises to 68
entries.summary: Indonesia marked its Independence Day on Monday but celebrations have been overshadowed by an earthquake which has left over 60 people dead and thousands homeless. Residents say they need aid as soon as possible.
entries.content:
Indonesia

Indonesia: Thousands await aid after earthquake kills 68

August 17, 2026

Indonesia marked its Independence Day on Monday but celebrations have been overshadowed by an earthquake which has left over 60 people dead and thousands homeless. Residents say they need aid as soon as possible.

The death toll from the 7.7-magnitude earthquake which hit eastern Indonesia this weekend rose to at least 68 on Monday, casting a shadow over the country's Independence Day celebrations.

Over 100 more people have been injured but local authorities do not believe anybody is missing.

The quake's epicenter was located off the coast of the island of Flores at a shallow depth of 10 kilometers (6.2 miles) on Saturday, the US Geological Survey (USGS) said.

It has since been followed by almost 1,600 smaller aftershocks, including a 5.6-magnitude jolt on Monday morning.

A tsunami warning for parts of East Nusa Tenggara, West Nusa Tenggara, South Sulawesi and Southeast Sulawesi provinces, urging residents to stay away from beaches and riverbanks, was later lifted.

But around 500 houses have been damaged and roads have been blocked by landslides, leaving around 12,800 people on Flores unable to return to their homes.

Indonesia residents: 'We need aid as soon as possible'

"Our houses are no longer inhabitable, because many have collapsed and are full of cracks, so we can't go inside anymore," one resident told the AFP news agency outside a self-made tent that was sleeping about 30 people.

"We only go back home to get water, clothes, pillows, and then we spend the nights here."

Other residents complained to the Reuters news agency about poor conditions in such tents, with some children contracting diarrhea and at least one older person suffering a stroke.

"I can only eat rice with nothing else," said one young mother whose baby was wrapped in a brown blanket in the back of a pickup truck. "We need aid as soon as possible. ⁠We are ​just salt farmers."

Indonesia: how is the government responding?

On Sunday evening, Indonesia's disaster mitigation agency, known as BNPB, said the Indonesian Air Force was preparing to bring 13 tons of emergency aid to the region.

The country's deputy health minister, Benjamin Paulus ⁠Octavianus, said the military was also planning to construct an emergency field hospital but said neurosurgeons and orthopedic surgeons were needed to treat head injuries and broken bones.

The earthquake is Indonesia's deadliest disaster since a 2022 quake killed hundreds in West Java, and has overshadowed the country's Independence Day celebrations marking independence from Japanese rule in 1945.

President Prabowo Subianto marked the occasion by presiding over celebrations in the capital, Jakarta, about 1,500 kilometers (930 miles) west of the ​disaster zone.

But the festivities were the last thing on the mind of residents affected by the earthquake, with one father telling Reuters: "I'm not thinking about that anymore. I'm just thinking about the safety of my wife and 4-year-old twins."

Indonesia's history of earthquakes

Indonesia is located on the so-called "Ring of Fire," a region of heightened seismic activity in the Pacific basin that stretches from Southeast Asia to Japan.

Here are some of the biggest earthquakes to strike the region:

  • 1992, magnitude 7: A tsunami following a strong earthquake on the southeastern island of Flores killed about 2,500 people
  • 2004, magnitude 9.1: A quake struck off the coast of Sumatra, triggering a tsunami that killed 170,000 in Indonesia and 220,000 in several countries in the Indian Ocean
  • 2018, magnitude 6.9: A tremor killed more than 550 people on the islands of Lombok and Sumbawa
  • 2018, magnitude 7.5: A quake and a subsequent tsunami in Palu on Sulawesi island left more than 4,300 people dead or missing

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: India's testing agency in focus after more exams canceled
entries.summary: Months after canceling the medical entrance exam, India's testing agency has canceled three other exams prompting outrage among opposition leaders. In Bihar, several people were killed in a temple stampede. DW has more
entries.content:
India

India's testing agency in focus after more exams canceled

Published August 17, 2026last updated August 17, 2026

Months after canceling the medical entrance exam, India's testing agency has canceled three other exams prompting outrage among opposition leaders. In Bihar, several people were killed in a temple stampede. DW has more

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • National Testing Agency cancels three exams for grant entrance tests over 'errors'
  • Opposition leaders call for education agency to be held accountable
  • Seven killed, several injured in temple stampede in Bihar
  • Eight pilgrims killed in hotel fire in West Bengal

Here's a roundup of the biggest headlines from India on Monday, August 17: 

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section India signs $203 million drone deal for Navy

India signs $203 million drone deal for Navy

India's Ministry of Defense on Monday said it signed a contract with US-based General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, leasing two remotely piloted aircraft systems for the Indian Navy.

The lease, for a period of 30 months, is valued at Rs 1,943 crore ($203 million, €175 million).

"The MQ-9B Sea Guardian HALE RPAS, equipped with advanced systems, state-of-the-art sensors and sophisticated payloads, will significantly enhance the Indian Navy's Maritime Domain Awareness capabilities," the ministry said, adding it would provide intelligence and cover vast maritime domains in the Indian Ocean.

The deal comes at a time when India and China are engaged in a strategic tussle for influence over the region.

The Indian Navy leased two MQ-9A Sea Guardian drones from General Atomics in 2020, a one-year deal which was later extended.

Skip next section PM Modi 'anguished' by deaths in Tarapith

PM Modi 'anguished' by deaths in Tarapith

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has extended his condolences to the families of those who lost their lives in the hotel fire in the temple town of Tarapith in eastern India.

"Anguished to hear about the loss of lives due to a fire tragedy in Birbhum, West Bengal," the prime minister's office quoted Modi as saying.

Birbhum is a district in the state of West Bengal and home to Tarapith, where tens of thousands of devotees gather at this time of year to mark the end of the holy month of Shravan.

"May the injured recover soon. The local administration is assisting those affected in the mishap," Modi said.

West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari and former Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee also expressed their "pain" and "shock" in social media posts.

As per Adhikari, at least eight people have died despite the police administration acting "swiftly" to rescue many. Five of the eight deceased were from the northeastern state of Meghalaya.

Skip next section WATCH: The tiger mystery that changed conservation in India

WATCH: The tiger mystery that changed conservation in India

The disappearance of tigers from Sariska Tiger Reserve in 2005 reshaped conservation in India.

Ecologist Ghazala Shahabuddin argued that poaching was only part of the story, pointing to habitat loss and environmental change. Her research led her to work closely with local communities, and later to co-found CEDAR, helping people document biodiversity and contribute local knowledge to wildlife conservation and forest protection.

Skip next section WATCH: Can a heat wave trigger a paycheck? India is trying it

WATCH: Can a heat wave trigger a paycheck? India is trying it

Millions of workers in India face a growing threat from extreme heat, but unlike floods or storms, heat often leaves no visible damage, only lost income. So what happens when rising temperatures make it impossible to work?

This report follows Shabnam, a tailor in Uttar Pradesh, and explores an unusual solution: insurance that pays workers automatically when temperatures cross a certain threshold.

Designed for informal workers, who often lack financial safety nets, the scheme is already helping thousands in India cope with heat-related income losses. But can a weather-triggered payout truly capture the realities of heat stress? From questions about fairness and affordability to the challenges of scaling heat wave insurance in a warming world, what can we learn from this bold experiment?

Skip next section Hotel fire kills 7 in West Bengal temple town

Hotel fire kills 7 in West Bengal temple town

A hotel fire in West Bengal's temple town of Tarapith left at least seven people dead and several others critically injured, Indian media reported.

The fire erupted at about 5 a.m. local time (2330 GMT Sunday) on the ground floor of a four-story hotel as most guests were asleep.

The Times of India reported that all seven victims died of asphyxiation from the smoke. The injured were being treated at a local hospital.

The temple town of Tarapith is currently more crowded than ususal as Monday marked the last day of the holy month of Shravan. The period typically draws large numbers of pilgrims to the town.

Skip next section India's opposition calls for NTA to be 'held accountable'

India's opposition calls for NTA to be 'held accountable'

In the hours after the NTA announced retests for the University Grants Commission - National Eligibility Test (UGC-NET), India's opposition leaders began once again pointing out alleged educational failures under Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

"Modi ji, look at what your NTA has just done," Rahul Gandhi, Modi's biggest political rival and leader of the opposition in the lower house of the parliament, said on X.

"This is no longer an education system. It is an extraction machine. It takes your money, your years, your mental health, and your confidence and returns nothing. Not even a job," Gandhi said.

"Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation was the first step, not the last. NTA's leadership must be held accountable too," he added.

Several other allied leaders echoed Gandhi on social media.

Some called for the resignation of NTA Chairperson Pradeep Kumar Joshi, while others called for the agency to be dissolved completely.

Prime Minister Modi installed party veteran Pralhad Joshi as India's new Education Minister on July 25, after Pradhan resigned under pressure of protests. The rare resignation was viewed as a dent in the government's invincibility aura, over 12 years into Modi's dominance in Indian politics. 

Modi has since sought to reassure students by announcing new student-friendly schemes and introducing legislation to increase punishment over paper leaks.

Skip next section India temple stampede in Bihar kills 7

India temple stampede in Bihar kills 7

A stampede at a temple in India's eastern Bihar state has left at least seven people dead and over a dozen injured, according to media reports.

The incident took place at the Ashok Dham temple in the Lakhisarai district as a swell of devotees thronged the site to offer water to Lord Shiva on what Hindus consider an auspicious Monday of the ongoing holy month of Shravan.

Shivam Kumar, a senior police officer, told news agency ANI that an electric pole fell at the site, sparking panic that led to the stampede.

He added that the incident was being investigated.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi expressed his grief over the deaths.

"My thoughts are with the bereaved families in this hour of grief. May the injured recover at the earliest. The local administration is assisting those affected," the prime minister's office quoted him as saying.

Read thefull story here.

Skip next section India's testing agency cancels three exams over 'errors'

India's testing agency cancels three exams over 'errors'

India's National Testing Agency (NTA) has canceled three entrance exams to test the eligibility of candidates for grants, PhDs and the position of assistant professors, after receiving complaints of significant errors in the question papers.

The exams for English, Commerce and Sociology will now be re-conducted in September, the NTA said in a statement.

The agency said it found that "the three papers had many factual, typographical, translation errors including misspelt names of prominent scholars, garbled book titles, errors in the stem wording of questions, grammatical errors, gender and number agreement errors, punctuation mistakes, and non-standard coined terms for established concepts, as well as repetition of a significant number of questions previously administered."

While the agency has waived the fee amount for the retests, students will likely face delayed plans, another round of studying and repeated uncertainty.

This comes months after the NTA canceled the all-India pre-medical NEET examination after its question paper was leaked. The re-examination reportedly drove tens of students to suicide and sparked youth-led protests across India, resulting in the resignation of then Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan in July.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello! Welcome to DW's India blog.

This is Mahima Kapoor reporting from the national capital where alleged failures in India's education system are still at the center of politics. That's weeks after protests forced the former education minister's resignation over leaked question papers from a crucial pre-medical entrance test. 

The National Testing Agency, which drew much of the public ire in July's protests, has now canceled three other entrance exams over several errors in the question papers. India's opposition leaders are now calling for the agency to be "held accountable."

In other news, a temple stampede in the state of Bihar killed at least seven people and has left dozens injured. Another seven pilgrims were killed in the neighboring state of West Bengal when a hotel caught fire in a popular temple town. 

Stay tuned for all of this and more!

entries.title: Fatty food raises risk of colorectal cancer
entries.summary: Did you know fatty foods can increase production of an acid in your gut that promotes tumor growth? That's on top of all the other health risks linked to fatty foods, like fries and burgers.
entries.content:
August 17, 2026

Did you know fatty foods can increase production of an acid in your gut that promotes tumor growth? That's on top of all the other health risks linked to fatty foods, like fries and burgers.

The list of health risks associated with foods high in fat and low in fiber is long:

  • low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL) or "bad" cholesterol
  • clogged arteries
  • weight gain
  • heart disease
  • liver stress
  • blood sugar spikes
  • bad digestion

And the list goes on.

Now a team of German researchers has shown how so-called Western diets that are often full of fatty foods can lead to the development of one of the most common — and deadliest — cancers in adults under 50 years of age.

The researchers from the Technical University of Munich, RWTH Aachen and the German Institute of Human Nutrition Potsdam-Rehbrücke (DIfE) found that these unhealthy diets sustain certain gut bacteria that produce a secondary bile acid — which in turn promotes tumor growth.

Their results were published in the August 2026 issue of the journal Gut.

"What's special about our study is that it shows the causality," Annika Osswald, the first author of the study and a PhD student at the German Institute of Human Nutrition, told DW. "Until now, we only knew there was some sort of connection between [a certain] secondary bile acid and colorectal cancer."

How bile acid is linked to colorectal cancer

The fat in the food you eat triggers the production of primary bile acids in your liver. These acids are important ― your body needs them to break down and absorb fats. Most of the primary bile acids are reabsorbed and returned to the liver.

But a small fraction reaches the colon, where certain bacteria convert them into secondary bile acids, including one called deoxycholic acid (DCA). The more fatty foods you eat, the higher the concentration of DCA in your colon. And that's where the problems start.

Osswald and her colleagues tested this in mice in a lab. "At the core of our work to prove causality were the mouse models," Osswald explained.

The research team implanted DCA-producing bacteria into mice whose intestinal microbiome they controlled completely. Then the scientists induced colorectal cancer in these mice, and also in mice without the bacteria. The mice that had DCA-producing bacteria in their gut saw more tumor growth than the mice that didn't have it.

Cell division in the mice with DCA was increased as well. Increased cell division makes it more likely for cancer to develop, because it multiplies the chances of DNA replication errors. These DNA mutations during cell division can stack up and lead to cancer.

To see whether the process they had observed in mice also takes place in humans, the researchers analyzed stool samples from more than a thousand people, both with and without colorectal cancer. Genes of DCA-producing bacteria were found more frequently in people with colorectal cancer.

"Our results show how much a Western high-fat diet and the associated changes in the gut microbiome can affect human gut health," said microbiologist Sören Ocvirk, another author of the study.

Osswald emphasizes that the team's work is foundational, and that more research needs to be done. Still, having proven the causality between more DCA-producing gut bacteria and increased tumor growth points to possible treatments of colorectal cancer as well.

Why it's vital to better understand colorectal cancer

Colorectal cancer is the only cancer for which the mortality rate in people under 50 years has increased in the past few decades. That's according to findings published in the Journal of the American Medical Association in January 2026.

The number of deaths from brain cancer, breast cancer, leukemia and lung cancer all went down in the US from 1990 to 2023. But the number of deaths from colorectal cancer increased by 1.1% annually, starting in 2005. While the US is only one region in the world, it is often considered a sufficient indicator of such trends, especially when it comes to the Western diet.

When detected early, cancer starting in the colon or the rectum is treatable.

But symptoms frequently don't present in the early stages of the disease. And when they do, they may be misinterpreted as indications of less harmful conditions like hemorrhoids or irritable bowel syndrome.

Symptoms for colorectal cancer include:

  • blood in or on your stool
  • intermittent or constant diarrhea or constipation
  • persistent abdominal pain
  • gas or cramps
  • feeling bloated

Another obstacle to early detection is that some people may feel embarrassed discussing colorectal health symptoms with their doctor.

So, try not to be embarrassed, talk to your doctor.

How can study results help with treating colorectal cancer?

One option to be considered in the future could be microbiome transplants.

"You could transplant the microbiome of people who have fewer DCA-producing bacteria in their gut into patients with colorectal cancer," Osswald said. "That could potentially slow down tumor growth."

But the best option is to prevent colorectal cancer in the first place. While some people may have a genetic disposition to developing colorectal cancer, a lot is down to lifestyle factors.

Eating healthily, reducing the amount of meat and fatty foods in your diet, and not smoking, are some good ways to decrease your colorectal cancer risk.

Edited by: Zulfikar Abbany

entries.title: Germany news: Belgium blaze kept out of Germany for now
entries.summary: Some residents in the Eifel town of Monschau were evacuated as a massive fire in Belgium threatened to cross the border. Meanwhile, shipping shortfalls amid low river water levels could hit the construction industry.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Belgium blaze kept out of Germany for now

Published August 17, 2026last updated August 17, 2026

Some residents in the Eifel town of Monschau were evacuated as a massive fire in Belgium threatened to cross the border. Meanwhile, shipping shortfalls amid low river water levels could hit the construction industry.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • A massive wildfire in Belgium has stopped its advance to the German border, firefighters say
  • Reduced cargo shipping on rivers amid low water levels could impact construction supplies, associations say
  • New statistics show one in 10 young people are not in work or training

Here is a roundup of top headlines from and about Germany on August 17, 2026:

Don't let the algorithm hide the news. If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google so you'll always see our verified news first.

Skip next section Mixed forests needed to lessen wildfire risk — Forestry Council

Mixed forests needed to lessen wildfire risk — Forestry Council

The head of the German Forestry Council has said Germany should urgently convert its conifer forests into mixed forests in the face of the growing wildfire threat as climate change advances.

Christian Haase told the public broadcaster Deutschlandfunk that the increased fire danger "means for us as forest owners: forest conversion, forest conversion, forest conversion."

"We must move away from pure conifer stands towards mixed forests," he said.

However, he conceded that the shift would take some time.

"This will certainly take another decade," he said.

Studies suggest that monocultural forests are more frequently affected and more severely affected by fires.

Pine forests in particular are considered highly flammable as their trees are rich in resins and oils.

Germany has seen several recent wildfires, including one in Hürtgen Forest that was the worst in the recorded history of the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia.

Skip next section People in Germany taking more domestic trips

People in Germany taking more domestic trips

In 2025, people in Germany cut the number of trips they took abroad, while the number of trips taken within the country with at least one overnight stay rose, figures from the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) showed on Monday.

The number of trips within Germany climbed by 3.9% in comparison with 2024 to 169 million, Destatis said.

Foreign travel went down by around 8.3% in comparison with the year before, to 105 million.

The most popular destination was Italy, followed by Austria, Spain, France and the Netherlands.

For all trips, the most popular means of transport was the car (60.2%), with rail (19.2%) and plane (15.2%) lagging well behind.

Skip next section Growing number of young people not in work or training

Growing number of young people not in work or training

The number of 20 to 24-year-olds in Germany who were neither employed nor doing training or studies rose to 10% in 2025 as part of a continuing trend, new figures have shown.

In 2022, the figure was 8.8%, the Federal Statistical Office said, using international comparative data from the European statistics authority Eurostat.

However, the figure from Germany is relatively low among all 27 EU nations and below the average of 12.9% for the bloc.

The Netherlands had the lowest percentage of people in the 20-24 age group who were unemployed or not doing some professional training, at 5.6%.

The figure was highest in Romania (22.8%), Bulgaria (17.3%) and France (16.2%).

Young people in rural areas of Germany were less likely than those in big cities to fall into the category (7.9% and 10.6% respectively).

Skip next section Low water levels in rivers could impact construction: industry associations

Low water levels in rivers could impact construction: industry associations

The building sector could face supply shortfalls as ships on German rivers carry less cargo because of falling water levels, construction industry associations say.

"Transport by water is becoming increasingly difficult," Thomas Reimann, the president of an association representing construction contractors in the German state of Hesse, told the DPA news agency.

He said that sand and gravel, which are often shipped in large quantities to concrete plants, are becoming harder to come by and more expensive.

The German Construction Industry Federation (HDB) also said suppliers had already warned that continued low water levels could lead to shortages in some building supplies.

Bitumen, aggregate, natural stone, fuels and mineral construction waste are among the other materials affected by the reduced shipping capacity.

HDB chief executive Tim-Oliver Müller said it was unlikely that construction would be brought to a widespread halt but that the risk of shortages, higher logistics costs and delays was growing as low water levels persist.

Skip next section Precautionary evacuations in Monschau as Belgium fire rages

Precautionary evacuations in Monschau as Belgium fire rages

Several homes in the Eifel town of Monschau were evacuated overnight as a wildfire burning in Belgium's High Fens nature reserve threatened to cross the border.

Around 30 residents from 17 homes were evacuated, with emergency accommodation set up at a nearby school.

However, by Monday morning the fire was said to have stopped its advance toward Germany amid weather conditions that are more favorable to firefighting efforts.

The fire had previously moved to within about 300 meters (984 feet) of the German border.

A spokesman for the local fire brigade said meadows between the fire and homes had been soaked with water for hours to help stop the spread of the flames.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

The DW newsroom in Bonn wishes guten Tag to its readers at the start of a new week.

Although the recent (very) hot weather in Germany seems to be over for now, the wildfire risk remains high, as is shown by the massive blaze in neighboring Belgium.

Some streets in the border town of Monschau were evacuated late on Sunday as the flames threatened to enter German territory, but they have fortunately been successfully held back for now.

The persistent dry conditions continued to pose problems to cargo shipping on the Rhine and other rivers, with construction associations saying that supplies could be delayed and are becoming more expensive.

entries.title: US actress Hayden Panettiere dies at 36
entries.summary: Hayden Panettiere's death was announced by her father in a statement to US network ABC news. The actress was known for her roles in TV shows such as "Nashville" and "Heroes."
entries.content:
August 17, 2026

Hayden Panettiere's death was announced by her father in a statement to US network ABC news. The actress was known for her roles in TV shows such as "Nashville" and "Heroes."

Hayden Panettiere, best known for her roles in US TV shows "Heroes" and "Nashville," has died aged 36, US media reports said.

"It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of our beloved Hayden. She was an incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy to all who knew her — and to the millions who watched her onscreen," Panettiere's father, Skip, was quoted by ABC news as saying.

The cause of Panettiere's death has not yet been announced. Her father has urged for privacy.

She would have turned 37 on Friday.

Who was Hayden Panettiere?

Panettiere began her career as a child actor, featuring in commercials and soap operas.

She gained ‌widespread recognition as the voice of Dot, the young princess ant in Pixar's 1998 animated success "A ​Bug's Life," and earned a Grammy nomination for the film's spoken word album for children.

Panettiere catapulted to fame with her role as Claire Bennett — a high school cheerleader ​with super powers — on NBC's television series "Heroes," which debuted in 2006 and went on to be a hit.

She also starred as up-and-coming country singer Juliette Barnes for six seasons on the musical drama "Nashville."

Panettiere also worked in two films of the horror "Scream" franchise, "Bring It On: All Or Nothing," "I Love You Beth Cooper" and "Remember the Titans."

Her last appearance was in the ​psychological thriller "Sleepwalker," which was released in ⁠the US in January.

Panettiere was vocal about her struggles

Panettiere was open about her struggles with alcohol addiction and depression.

She revealed that she had had dealt with addiction through her 20s.

Her younger brother — actor Jansen Panettiere — died in 2023 at 28 due to a heart condition.

Hayden's memoir was published earlier this year, where she spoke about her battle with mental health, the loss of her brother, and her decision to give full custody of her daughter to her former partner, Ukrainian boxer Wladimir Klitschko.

Edited by: Natalie Muller
